title: Autoscale safeguard: metric decorrelation and eviction workflow postmortem
creator: Miguel Ortega
description: Summary: During a regional traffic spike on 2026-02-24 we observed sustained underprovisioning in the inference serving tier. The net effect was elevated latencies and several customer-facing 503s for a 45 minute window. This postmortem analyzes why HPA/KEDA did not scale aggressively despite clear traffic growth and documents the mitigations we implemented.<n><n>What happened: Our KEDA scalers are fed by a proxy-level metric stream (requests-in-flight + queue depth) that aggregates multiplexed connections across many logical tenants. During the spike the proxy introduced short-lived connection churn (TCP resets and HTTP/2 stream reassignments) which produced high-frequency variance in individual metric samples. Our percentile-based smoothing (90th over 1m) together with an alignment window meant the aggregated signal decorrelated from actual sustained request arrivals, causing KEDA to underreport demand (false negatives). Concurrently, node-level eviction logic reclaimed warm buffer pods when node pressure spiked, removing warm caches and increasing cold-start latency, further worsening user-visible latency. The combination created a feedback loop: underscale -> higher latency -> more request timeouts -> metric noise -> continued underscale.

root_cause: Two orthogonal issues combined: (1) signal decorrelation from proxy-level metric aggregation plus short sampling windows caused percentile smoothing to produce false negatives for KEDA scalers; (2) aggressive node eviction/eviction-thresholds removed warm cache pods during high memory pressure, enabling cold starts that amplified latency and timeouts, feeding back into noisy scaler signals.
detection_and_response: Detection came from SLO dashboards and error rate pages. The on-call runbook directed to check scaler replica counts; we initially attempted to increase KEDA scalers' sensitivity but reverted to a manual minReplicas increase to stop customer impact. Post-incident, we ran additional load replays against a staging cluster to reproduce the signal decorrelation pattern and validated mitigations.
consequences: ~45 minutes of elevated 95/99p latency and ~0.8% customer-facing errors for affected routes. Several customers reported degraded experience; internal billing/usage spikes were observed for some workloads due to retries.
action_items:
1) Implement per-pool signal isolation: split proxy metrics for scaler inputs by logical serving pool to avoid cross-tenant noise. (Owner: Ava Chen; ETA: 2026-03-15)
2) Replace rolling 90th percentile over 1m with a hybrid confidence score: EMA of rate + percentile smoothing with outlier dampening. Prototype in canary cluster. (Owner: Miguel Ortega; ETA: 2026-03-22)
3) Add a short "scale confidence" hold window (30s) that requires successive high-confidence samples before scale-down is allowed; scale-up remains aggressive. (Owner: Reliability team; ETA: 2026-03-12)
4) Adjust node eviction thresholds for warm-cache pods: mark warm-cache pods with evictionPriority=low and reserve a minimal memory headroom for these pods. (Owner: Infra; ETA: 2026-03-18)
5) Create an automated chaos test that injects proxy-level stream churn and validates scaler responsiveness in CI. (Owner: SRE; ETA: 2026-04-02)
6) Dashboard and alert tuning: add a "scale confidence" metric and an alert when scaler input variance exceeds a threshold. (Owner: Observability; ETA: 2026-03-08)
resolution_summary: Completed short-term manual mitigations during the incident (minReplicas bump). Implemented scale confidence hold window and dashboard alerts (merged PRs). Scoped the per-pool metric split and confidence-score prototype; prototype validated in canary and scheduled for rollout. Eviction threshold changes scheduled for next infra maintenance window.

follow_up_notes: We learned that aggregated signals that span multiplexed networking layers can hide sustained demand when the lower-level transport exhibits short-lived churn. Long-term, we should move scaler inputs as close to the serving layer (per-worker) as feasible or compute a 'routing-aware' aggregate that weights stable connections more heavily. The confidence-score approach is a middle ground that allows us to tune sensitivity without immediate architectural changes.
